title: "Computerized System Validation & BECS"

## The finish line

By the end of this course you can pick up a validation package for BECS (Blood Establishment
Computer Software) or a system that touches it, and judge whether it would hold up. That means
the requirements (URS and FRS: user and functional requirements specifications), the
installation, operational, and performance qualification evidence (IQ, OQ, PQ), and the
traceability matrix that ties them together. You'll also be able to say where BECS sits under
FDA's medical-device quality system rules. Spoiler: those device rules bind your vendor, not
you (unless you start building BECS software yourself), and knowing why changes what you ask
that vendor for.

You've already been told twice that this course was coming. In
[BECS in the pipeline](../blood-center-operations/becs-in-the-pipeline/index.qmd) you learned
*why* a routine OS patch on the BECS server needed a validation impact assessment. In
[Reviewing a validation package](../directing-the-quality-analyst/reviewing-validation-packages/index.qmd)
you reviewed that assessment, VIA-0842, for its decision trail. One question was left open on
purpose: were twelve targeted tests actually enough? This course gives you the method to answer
it, and then answers it.

## Before you start

This course assumes the three foundations and the first course:

- [Reading a CFR citation](../../foundations/reading-a-cfr-citation/index.qmd)
- [Regulatory landscape orientation](../../foundations/regulatory-landscape-orientation/index.qmd)
  — you'll need it constantly here. This course mixes FDA regulation, FDA guidance, an
  international standard (ISO 13485), and industry practice (GAMP 5, IQ/OQ/PQ), and mixing
  them up is the most common mistake in validation documents.
- [Risk and controls vocabulary](../../foundations/risk-and-controls-vocabulary/index.qmd)
  — validation effort scales with risk. Likelihood, severity, and detectability do real work
  in modules 1 and 6.
- [Blood Center Operations](../blood-center-operations/index.qmd), especially
  [BECS in the pipeline](../blood-center-operations/becs-in-the-pipeline/index.qmd). Its
  definition of BECS (the system behind eligibility, release, labeling, and disposition) is
  the one this course uses.

Strongly recommended, because this course picks up their open threads:

- [Change control for regulated systems](../quality-system-essentials/change-control-for-regulated-systems/index.qmd)
  from [Quality System Essentials](../quality-system-essentials/index.qmd). Module 6 assumes
  you know the change-control stages and doesn't re-teach them.
- [Reviewing a validation package: the decision trail](../directing-the-quality-analyst/reviewing-validation-packages/index.qmd)
  from [Directing the Quality Analyst](../directing-the-quality-analyst/index.qmd). Its
  cold-read test is the first half of every review in this course. This course adds the
  second half.

## The seven modules

Each module is one sitting, and each has its own finish line.

1. **How much validation, and why: GAMP 5 and the V-model.** Sort any BECS component into
   its GAMP 5 software category, walk the V-model from requirements to the tests that answer
   them, and explain why a risk assessment, not the category, sets how hard you test.
2. **IQ, OQ, PQ, and the traceability matrix.** Read an executed validation package and judge
   whether every high-risk requirement was tested in a way that could fail, under the
   conditions it will really run in, with every failure explained. Then say whether the
   package is defensible.
3. **BECS as a regulated device.** Explain what makes BECS a medical device under FDA rules,
   what a 510(k) clearance does and doesn't tell you about the version you run, and what FDA's
   BECS validation guidance expects your own validation to add, at every site.
4. **The vendor's quality system: QMSR and ISO 13485.** Say which quality rules bind the BECS
   manufacturer and which bind Lakeshore, what device-grade evidence you can ask the vendor
   for, and when building your own software could make *you* the manufacturer.
5. **Part 11 for validated systems.** Name the electronic-records controls a BECS validation
   has to prove the system enforces, explain where FDA actually focuses enforcement of
   validation, and decide whether a vendor-supported BECS is still a "closed system."
6. **Staying validated: changes, patches, and periodic review.** Run any change, including an
   OS patch, through regression analysis and right-sized regression testing, design a
   periodic review that catches drift, and finally answer whether VIA-0842's twelve tests
   were enough.
7. **Interfaces and data across systems.** Follow data across every BECS boundary
   (instrument results in, labels out, reference tables in, shipment data out to hospitals,
   legacy data converted) and judge whether the interface validation and monitoring prove
   each record lands complete, correct, on time, and on the right donor or unit.

## What this course finally delivers

Two earlier modules stopped at a line on purpose, and said so.

`BECS in the pipeline` explained why BECS changes need a validation impact assessment and
Quality's blocking sign-off. It named GAMP 5, IQ/OQ/PQ, and FDA's BECS validation guidance but
didn't teach any of them. Modules 1 through 3 do.

`Reviewing a validation package` taught you to check the decision trail: scope, criteria set
before testing, failures recorded, approvals before deployment. It told you to route "was the
testing *enough*?" to Quality's validation lead, because you didn't yet have the method to
judge it yourself. Modules 2 and 6 give you that method. Module 6 applies it to VIA-0842, and
module 7 closes the interface testing VIA-0842 left as "to follow."

You still won't be the validation engineer. You'll be the system owner who can tell a
package that proves something from one that only looks finished, and who can say exactly what
is missing.

## A note on sources

This course leans on more kinds of source than any before it, so keep the labels straight:

- **FDA regulation** (binding): the CFR sections behind BECS validation and device
  classification, quoted from local copies.
- **FDA guidance** (FDA's current thinking, "should" language): chiefly *Blood Establishment
  Computer System Validation in the User's Facility* (CBER, April 2013), quoted from a local
  copy.
- **International standard**: ISO 13485, which FDA's device quality rule incorporates by
  reference. It's copyrighted, so it's named and described here, never quoted.
- **Industry practice**: GAMP 5 (ISPE) and the IQ/OQ/PQ vocabulary. Widely used and
  defensible, but not law. Also copyrighted, so it's described in this course's own words.

Modules appear in the sidebar as they're built.
